SEC23A-01.note: Inverted after 'Rarely'; subject is the plural 'saplings' and the participle 'grown' far downstream needs perfect 'have'. 'terraces' and 'orchard' pull toward has/does, and do/does only fail once 'grown' is reached.

SEC23A-02.note: Verb agrees with singular 'coat' (shields); the embryos belong to the seeds, so 'their'. 'shields its' (C) is the strongest distractor, readable as the coat's embryos, but the coat has no embryos of its own.

SEC23A-03.note: 'Many a' takes a singular verb; the generic present ('if the rash appears') gives 'is'. 'are' tempts through the plural sense of 'many'.

SEC23A-04.note: An absolute phrase sits between the plural subject 'twins' and the verb; 'review' fixes the present, so 'are breathing'. The singular 'sensor/infant' right before the blank pulls toward 'is'.

SEC23A-05.note: The head noun is plural 'swabs'; 'when the fungus appeared' fixes the past, so 'were shipped'. 'laboratory' in the comparative phrase pulls toward 'was'.

SEC23A-06.note: The subject is singular 'Biochar'; the 'or ...' phrase is a renaming appositive and does not make it plural. 'until the autumn rains return' sets the present. The plural 'fragments' pulls toward 'are'.

SEC23A-07.note: 'for' (meaning because) is a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses, so it takes a comma. B misreads 'for' as a preposition and garbles the sentence; a semicolon or colon before a FANBOYS is out on the SAT (semicolon struck on sight).

SEC23A-08.note: 'both ... and' correlative with parallel 'in' phrases takes no comma. The comma in A is attractive because the first element is long; C (semicolon + and) is struck on sight.

SEC23B-01.note: Inversion after a fronted 'Of greater concern' phrase; the true subject 'seams' sits far downstream after three adjectives, and 'came up' fixes the past. A singular reading of 'concern' pulls toward was/is.

SEC23B-02.note: 'All that survives' is singular (the passage itself prints 'survives'); 'when ... closed' names a specific past time, which rules out the present perfect. 'instruments' pulls toward the plural.

SEC23B-03.note: 'The former' is the single anemometer; habitual 'whenever a storm brings' gives the present. 'pines' and the plural rain gauges pull toward 'are'.

SEC23B-04.note: The 'not the steady breeze' interrupter does not change the plural subject 'footsteps'; 'crossed' fixes the past. 'breeze' right before the blank pulls toward 'was'.

SEC23B-05.note: 'the longest of which' means one tunnel, so singular; 'until groundwater broke' fixes the past. 'which' standing for 'four tunnels' pulls toward 'were'.

SEC23B-06.note: An elliptical comparison: the stand-in verb must replace 'holds' (so do, not be) and agree with plural 'terraces'. 'does' tempts through matching 'loess'; 'are' tempts because comparisons often end in a form of be.

SEC23B-07.note: 'most broke apart within seconds' is an independent clause; a semicolon joins it, a comma alone is a splice. A tempts because the infinitive phrase makes the first clause feel like an intro. D (comma pair around 'most') is garbled.

SEC23B-08.note: A complete clause ending in 'three common minerals' introduces the list, so a colon. With a comma (B) the three names read as more items in the outer list; a semicolon before a list is never right.

SEC23C-01.note: A 'So quickly ... that' inversion: the subject is singular 'slang' with the progressive 'spreading', so 'is'. 'schools/leagues' pull toward plural, and does/do only fail at 'spreading'.

SEC23C-02.note: 'which' takes the compound 'both the altarpiece and the choir screen' (and 'side by side' confirms it), so plural; 'compare' gives the present. 'choir screen' just before the blank pulls toward singular.

SEC23C-03.note: The head noun is 'hypothesis', so both the verb and the pronoun are singular. The plural 'scribes'/'workshop' clause invites 'owe their' or a mixed choice.

SEC23C-04.note: 'The founder and first director' (one article) is one person, confirmed later by 'she', so singular; 'suffered' fixes the past. The 'X and Y' compound strongly pulls toward 'were'.

SEC23C-05.note: A concessive 'Faded as X are' with plural 'frescoes'; the main clause's present 'is easy' keeps it present. 'is' tempts because it echoes the main clause and 'subject'; 'were' is weaker, since the fading is a present condition.

SEC23C-06.note: The object 'This last ledger' is fronted; the subject is plural 'archivists' and 'when a burst pipe flooded' requires the past progressive. The fronted singular 'ledger' pulls toward was/has.

SEC23C-07.note: An interrupter that holds its own commas is set off by a matched pair of dashes. A (comma pair) is the strongest distractor but leaves the list indistinguishable from the subject; D's dash-comma mismatch and C's unpunctuated run are struck on sight.

SEC23C-08.note: With three engravers, 'Vidal' is the information that identifies which one, so it is a restrictive appositive with no commas. A (comma pair) is the attractive choice, treating the name as extra; B and C put a lone comma between the subject and its verb or the name.

tells: Two-by-two grids (singular/plural x past/present, or verb x pronoun) cover 18 of 24 items. The key letters spread evenly (6 each A-D), so letter position is no tell.

In many agreement items the noun right before the blank has the WRONG number for the key (A-04 infant, A-05 laboratory, A-06 fragments, B-02 instruments, B-03 pines, B-04 breeze, C-01 leagues, C-02 choir screen, C-06 ledger). 'Pick the number opposite the nearest noun' scores well but fails A-01, A-03 and B-05, so it is a partial heuristic.
Tense is always fixed by a nearby when/until/as/whenever clause or a parallel main verb (past when the clause is past, present otherwise). This is a consistent cue but it is the rule, not a shortcut.
Boundary items: a semicolon option paired with a FANBOYS or a list (A-07 A, A-08 C, B-08 D) is never the key; a mismatched or lone-comma option (C-07 D, C-08 B/C, B-07 D) always loses.

phase2_note: All 24 keys match my cold answers (0 cold misses), and every explanation's path produces its key and rejects each distractor correctly. Minor wording issues only: SEC23C-07 says the list 'must' take dashes, which overstates it; parentheses would also work and none are offered, but the comma pair is correctly rejected as ambiguous. SEC23A-07 calls a semicolon or colon before 'for' unconventional, which matches SAT practice. No per-item drops. The batch-level risk is template repetition: 18 of 24 are 2x2 agreement grids (see near_duplicates), and the plural/singular attractor next to the blank recurs.
